triage.name: Chickenpox
triage.reason: Highly recognizable exanthem with a classic prodrome and rash progression; diagnosis made clinically by history and exam.

risk_factors.text: No prior chickenpox and no varicella vaccination
Close contact with a person who has chickenpox or shingles
Household exposure to an infectious person

comorbidities: Chronic skin conditions such as eczema
social_history: Recent travel or contact with a person who had a rash
exposures: Contact with a person who has chickenpox
Contact with a person who has shingles
Household member with a vesicular rash

chief_complaints.text: I have an itchy rash with blisters
My child has spots all over

hpi.onset: Rash often appears first in children; a mild prodrome of fever and malaise may occur 1 to 2 days before the rash, especially in adults
hpi.duration: Illness usually lasts 4 to 7 days; new lesions stop appearing after about 4 to 5 days
hpi.progression: Rash begins as red macules and papules that rapidly become fluid-filled vesicles, then pustules and crusts; crops of lesions appear over several days so lesions in different stages are present at the same time
hpi.location: Starts on the chest, back and face, then spreads to the rest of the body, including the scalp, mouth and genital area; most concentrated on the chest and back
hpi.quality: Itchy, uncomfortable rash with fluid-filled blisters that break easily and scab over
hpi.severity: Usually mild in healthy children; more severe in infants, adolescents, adults, pregnant women and immunocompromised people
hpi.timing: Lesions appear in successive crops over 2 to 4 days; itching is continuous and worse at night
pertinent_negatives: Rash that stays in one dermatome
Rash that is only on the palms and soles
Blood in the stool or vomit
Recent aspirin use in a child

positives.text: Sores in the mouth or genital area

negatives: Rash limited to one side of the body
Rash only on the palms and soles
Severe sore throat with white patches

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants may have a higher fever and more widespread rash; they can become dehydrated from poor feeding and are at higher risk of complications.
Adults often have a more severe prodrome with high fever, severe malaise, headache and body aches before the rash; they are at higher risk of pneumonia and other complications.
Pregnant women who are not immune can have more severe disease and are at risk of varicella pneumonia; infection near delivery can cause severe neonatal varicella.
Lesions may be more numerous, atypical, hemorrhagic or continue to appear for longer; the rash may not crust normally and can involve internal organs.
missing_classic_features: Typical crops of vesicles that crust within a week

atypical.how_it_differs: Vaccinated children who develop breakthrough varicella usually have a milder illness with fewer than 50 lesions, low or no fever, and a rash that is more maculopapular than vesicular.
missing_classic_features: Lesions in all stages of development

general.mild: Alert, playful, nontoxic; comfortable between itching episodes
general.moderate: Irritable and uncomfortable, scratching frequently, mildly ill-appearing
general.severe: Ill-appearing, febrile and miserable, reluctant to move or be examined
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic or inconsolable, with labored breathing or altered mental status

findings.maneuver: Inspect the entire skin surface, including the scalp, mouth, palms, soles and genital area
findings.finding: Generalized pruritic rash with fluid-filled vesicles on an erythematous base

findings.maneuver: Inspect the rash closely for the stages of individual lesions
findings.finding: Macules, papules, vesicles, pustules and crusts present at the same time

findings.maneuver: Compare lesion density on the trunk with the extremities
findings.finding: Lesions most concentrated on the chest, back and face, with fewer on the extremities

findings.maneuver: Part the hair and inspect the scalp
findings.finding: Vesicles and crusted lesions on the scalp

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa, palate and posterior pharynx
findings.finding: Shallow ulcers or vesicles on the palate, buccal mucosa or tongue

findings.maneuver: Inspect the genital and perineal skin when the history or distribution suggests it
findings.finding: Vesicles or crusted lesions on the genital or perineal skin

findings.maneuver: Inspect for scratch marks and broken vesicles
findings.finding: Excoriation and ruptured vesicles from scratching

findings.maneuver: Map the distribution of the rash relative to dermatomes
findings.finding: Rash is widespread and does not follow a single dermatome
Rash is not limited to the palms and soles

findings.maneuver: Apply gentle lateral pressure to the edge of a blister
findings.finding: No sheet-like separation of the epidermis (Nikolsky sign absent)

findings.maneuver: Inspect individual lesions for concentric color rings
Palpate the cervical, axillary and inguinal lymph node chains
Auscultate the lungs and assess respiratory effort
findings.finding: Tachypnea, crackles or decreased breath sounds suggesting varicella pneumonia

findings.maneuver: Assess neck stiffness and perform a brief neurologic screen
findings.finding: Neck stiffness, photophobia or focal neurologic deficit suggesting CNS involvement

findings.maneuver: Assess level of consciousness and orientation

findings.finding: Soft, nontender abdomen without guarding or rebound

labs.caveat: The white count is often normal or mildly low in uncomplicated varicella; marked leukocytosis suggests bacterial superinfection, and leukopenia can occur with severe or disseminated disease.
Relative lymphocytosis is common in viral exanthems and is nonspecific.
Thrombocytopenia is uncommon and suggests severe or disseminated disease.
Transaminases may rise mildly with varicella; marked elevation suggests hepatitis or disseminated disease.
Mild transaminitis is common; marked elevation suggests hepatitis or disseminated disease.
Nonspecific; a high or rising value suggests bacterial superinfection such as cellulitis or pneumonia.
Helps distinguish bacterial superinfection from viral varicella when the picture is unclear.
Only if CNS involvement is suspected; a lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose supports viral meningoencephalitis.
Only if CNS involvement is suspected; mild protein elevation is typical of viral meningoencephalitis.
Only if CNS involvement is suspected; normal or mildly low glucose favors a viral cause over bacterial meningitis.

imaging.preferred_when: Adults or immunocompromised patients with respiratory symptoms

findings.text: Diffuse bilateral reticulonodular or patchy alveolar opacities
Normal chest x-ray despite symptoms (early disease)

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected varicella pneumonia when chest x-ray is normal or equivocal
Altered mental status or focal neurologic deficit

findings.text: Hypodense lesions in the basal ganglia or cortex (vasculopathy, encephalitis)

imaging.study: MRI brain with and without contrast

findings.text: T2 hyperintensities in the cerebellum, basal ganglia or cortex

initial.why: Assesses for leukocytosis suggesting bacterial superinfection or leukopenia in severe disease
Checks hydration and electrolytes in patients with poor intake or vomiting
Supports concern for bacterial superinfection when elevated

initial.only_if: respiratory symptoms, hypoxia or an immunocompromised adult

confirmatory.test: Vesicle fluid PCR for varicella-zoster virus
confirmatory.why: Most sensitive and specific test; confirms varicella when the diagnosis is uncertain or the patient is immunocompromised
Rapid confirmation from a vesicle scraping when PCR is unavailable
confirmatory.only_if: PCR is not available and rapid confirmation is needed

supporting.why: Can support recent infection or document immunity, but is less reliable than direct viral testing

supporting.only_if: CNS involvement is suspected (severe headache, stiff neck, confusion, seizures or focal deficit)

supporting.test: MRI brain with and without contrast

not_indicated.why: Not needed unless there is altered mental status or a focal neurologic deficit
not_indicated.only_if: altered mental status or focal neurologic deficit

not_indicated.why: Not routinely needed; reserve for suspected bacterial superinfection or sepsis
not_indicated.only_if: bacterial superinfection or sepsis is suspected

not_indicated.why: No role in the evaluation of chickenpox
No role in the evaluation of chickenpox

decision_points: Diagnosis is usually clinical; reserve PCR or DFA for uncertain, atypical, immunocompromised or pregnant cases
Consider chest imaging and antiviral therapy in adults or immunocompromised patients with respiratory symptoms
Lumbar puncture and brain imaging if CNS involvement is suspected
Do not use aspirin in children because of the risk of Reye syndrome

differential.name: Herpes zoster (shingles)
differential.why_considered: Same virus, vesicular rash on an erythematous base

history: Pain, burning or tingling precedes the rash in one area
Rash stays on one side of the body
Often in an adult or older adult rather than a child
exam: Vesicles confined to a single dermatome
Does not cross the midline
No crops of lesions in different stages elsewhere
labs: VZV PCR from a lesion can confirm either, so it does not separate them

differential.name: Smallpox
differential.why_considered: Febrile illness with a widespread vesicular then pustular rash
differential.trigger: Severe prodrome with high fever and a rash that starts on the face and extremities and is concentrated there, especially in an unvaccinated traveler

history: High fever and severe headache for 2 to 4 days before the rash
No known exposure to chickenpox
Travel to an area where smallpox could occur
exam: Lesions all in the same stage of development
Rash concentrated on the face and extremities (centrifugal) rather than the trunk
Lesions on the palms and soles
labs: Orthopoxvirus PCR from lesion fluid or scab at a public health laboratory

differential.name: Disseminated herpes simplex virus infection
differential.why_considered: Widespread vesicular rash with fever, especially in immunocompromised patients or neonates
differential.trigger: Neonate, pregnant patient or immunocompromised patient with grouped vesicles and systemic illness

history: Known HSV infection or recent genital or oral lesions
Neonate within the first weeks of life
Immunocompromising condition or medication
exam: Grouped vesicles rather than crops in different stages
Mucosal or genital lesions
May have hepatitis or encephalitis features
labs: HSV PCR positive from lesion, blood or CSF

differential.name: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease
differential.why_considered: Child with fever and a vesicular rash

history: Sores in the mouth with poor intake
Rash mainly on the hands and feet
Often after contact with another child with the same illness
exam: Vesicles concentrated on the palms, soles and mouth
Few or no lesions on the trunk
Rash does not follow crops in different stages

differential.name: Measles
differential.why_considered: Febrile viral exanthem in an unvaccinated child

history: Cough, runny nose and red eyes before the rash
Rash starts on the face and spreads downward
No itching
exam: Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa
Maculopapular rash rather than vesicles
Conjunctivitis

differential.name: Scabies
differential.why_considered: Intensely itchy rash in a child

history: Itching worse at night
Other family members itching
Itching for weeks rather than days
exam: Burrows in the finger webs, wrists and waist
Papules and excoriations rather than fluid-filled vesicles
No fever

differential.name: Impetigo
differential.why_considered: Honey-crusted skin lesions in a child

history: Lesions start as small blisters that break and form golden crusts
Often around the nose and mouth
No widespread crops of vesicles
exam: Honey-colored crusts
Lesions limited to a few areas
No lesions in the mouth or scalp

differential.name: Stevens-Johnson syndrome
differential.why_considered: Widespread blistering rash with mucosal involvement and fever
differential.trigger: Recent new medication with painful skin, mucosal erosions and skin that peels with gentle pressure

history: New medication in the past 1 to 3 weeks
Painful skin and mouth
Illness progressing quickly
exam: Skin separates with gentle lateral pressure (positive Nikolsky sign)
Large areas of denuded skin
Severe mucosal erosions of the mouth, eyes or genitals
labs: No specific laboratory test; diagnosis is clinical
Electrolyte and fluid losses may be present

severity.mild: Healthy child with fewer than 50 lesions, low or no fever, mild itching and no complications; often breakthrough varicella in a vaccinated child
severity.moderate: Typical unvaccinated child with widespread itchy vesicles in crops, fever up to about 102°F, malaise and poor appetite but drinking well
severity.severe: Adolescent, adult, infant or pregnant patient with high fever, hundreds of lesions, severe itching, mouth sores limiting intake, or early bacterial skin infection
severity.critical: Varicella pneumonia with hypoxia, encephalitis with altered mental status, disseminated disease with organ involvement, or sepsis from bacterial superinfection

red_flags.finding: Trouble breathing, chest pain or low oxygen saturation
red_flags.meaning: Varicella pneumonia, more common in adults, pregnant patients and immunocompromised patients

red_flags.finding: Confusion, severe headache, stiff neck, seizures or trouble walking
Rapidly spreading redness, warmth, swelling or pain in the skin
red_flags.meaning: Bacterial superinfection such as cellulitis or necrotizing fasciitis

red_flags.finding: High fever that returns after the rash has started to crust
Unable to drink, decreased urine output, lethargy
red_flags.meaning: Dehydration, especially in infants and young children

red_flags.finding: Bleeding into the skin, blood in vomit or stool
red_flags.meaning: Severe or disseminated disease with thrombocytopenia

red_flags.finding: Rash in a newborn whose mother had chickenpox around delivery
red_flags.meaning: Neonatal varicella, which can be severe

complications.name: Bacterial skin and soft tissue infection
clues: Increasing redness, warmth or pain around lesions
High fever after the rash has started to crust

complications.name: Varicella pneumonia
clues: Cough, shortness of breath or chest pain

complications.name: Congenital varicella syndrome
clues: Maternal infection in the first half of pregnancy
Limb or eye abnormalities on prenatal ultrasound

complications.name: Neonatal varicella
clues: Mother developed rash from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery
Newborn with widespread lesions and fever

complications.name: Shingles later in life
clues: Painful vesicular rash in a single dermatome years after chickenpox

special_populations.differences: Usually mild and self-limited; the main risks are dehydration from mouth sores and bacterial skin infection from scratching.
Higher fever and more widespread rash; poor feeding can lead to dehydration; higher risk of complications.
More severe prodrome with high fever and body aches; higher risk of varicella pneumonia and hospitalization.
Higher risk of severe varicella pneumonia; infection near delivery can cause severe neonatal varicella; early infection can rarely cause congenital varicella syndrome.
Lesions may be more numerous, atypical, hemorrhagic or continue to appear for longer; risk of disseminated disease involving the lungs, liver and brain.

key_questions.question: What does the rash look like, and has it changed since it started?
key_questions.looking_for: Red spots that quickly become fluid-filled blisters and then scabs; lesions in different stages at the same time

key_questions.question: Where did the rash start, and where has it spread?
key_questions.looking_for: Starts on the chest, back and face, then spreads over the body; most concentrated on the trunk

key_questions.question: Is the rash itchy?
key_questions.looking_for: Itchy; a rash that does not itch argues against chickenpox

key_questions.question: When did the rash start, and are new spots still appearing?
key_questions.looking_for: New crops over 2 to 4 days, then no new lesions; illness lasts about 4 to 7 days

key_questions.question: Did you have fever, tiredness or headache before the rash appeared?
key_questions.looking_for: Mild prodrome 1 to 2 days before the rash, especially in adults; in children the rash is often first

key_questions.question: Have you had chickenpox before, or have you received the chickenpox vaccine?
key_questions.looking_for: No prior chickenpox and no or incomplete vaccination; prior disease makes chickenpox unlikely

key_questions.question: Has anyone around you had chickenpox, a similar rash, or shingles?
key_questions.looking_for: Close contact with chickenpox or shingles 10 to 21 days before the rash; household or school exposure

key_questions.question: Do you take any medicines that weaken the immune system, such as steroids or biologics?
key_questions.looking_for: Corticosteroids, methotrexate, biologics or other immunosuppressants, which raise the risk of severe disease

key_questions.question: Do you have any condition that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Leukemia, lymphoma, HIV, transplant or other immunocompromising condition

key_questions.question: Are you pregnant, or could you be pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy without immunity, which raises the risk of severe varicella pneumonia and neonatal varicella

key_questions.question: Is it hard to breathe, or do you have chest pain or a cough?
key_questions.looking_for: Respiratory symptoms suggesting varicella pneumonia, especially in adults, pregnant or immunocompromised patients

key_questions.question: Any severe headache, stiff neck, confusion, seizures or trouble walking?
key_questions.looking_for: CNS involvement such as encephalitis, cerebellitis or meningitis

key_questions.question: Are you able to drink, and are you urinating normally?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor intake or decreased urine output suggesting dehydration, especially with mouth sores

key_questions.question: Have you given a child aspirin during this illness?
key_questions.looking_for: Aspirin use in a child, which risks Reye syndrome

Consider complications such as bacterial skin infection, pneumonia, encephalitis and dehydration

Itchy rash with vesicles and crusts in different stages at the same time
Rash starting on the trunk and spreading outward
Low-grade fever and malaise with the rash

Adult with a severe prodrome of high fever, headache and body aches before the rash

Rash with excoriation and early bacterial skin infection from scratching
